lead: An LSTM is a recurrent cell with gates that decide what to keep, what to write, and what to show. A plain RNN overwrites its hidden state at every step, so information from many steps ago fades. LSTM adds a cell state and sigmoid gates that act like taps. The same idea powers speech recognition, language modelling, handwriting recognition and time-series prediction, especially where the useful signal is many steps behind the current input.
prereq: You need: recurrence and unfolding in 4.2, gradients through time in 4.3, and sigmoid and tanh from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A plain RNN has one hidden state and overwrites it at every step. LSTM adds a second state, the cell state c_t, and three gates. A gate is a vector with entries between 0 and 1. It works like a tap: 0 blocks, 1 passes. Each gate is computed from the input x_t and the previous hidden state h_{t-1}.
The forget gate f_t scales the old cell state. The input gate i_t scales a new candidate c~_t. The output gate o_t scales the squashed cell state to form h_t.
f_t = σ(W_f x_t + U_f h_{t-1} + b_f)
blocks.where: f_t is the forget gate vector at step t; x_t is the input; h_{t-1} is the previous hidden state; W_f and U_f are weight matrices; b_f is a bias vector; σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) gives entries in (0,1).

blocks.text:
i_t = σ(W_i x_t + U_i h_{t-1} + b_i)
c~_t = tanh(W_c x_t + U_c h_{t-1} + b_c)
c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c~_t
o_t = σ(W_o x_t + U_o h_{t-1} + b_o)
h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t)
blocks.where: i_t is the input gate; c~_t is the candidate cell state; c_t is the new cell state; c_{t-1} is the previous cell state; o_t is the output gate; h_t is the new hidden state; ⊙ is elementwise multiplication; tanh squashes each entry to (−1,1); W_i, U_i, W_c, U_c, W_o, U_o are weight matrices; b_i, b_c, b_o are bias vectors.

sections.h3: Why the additive cell path helps

blocks.text: The cell state uses addition, not a matrix product: c_t = f_t⊙c_{t-1} + i_t⊙c~_t. During backpropagation through time, error can travel from c_t to c_{t-1} through the factor f_t. If f_t is near 1, that factor is near 1, so the error is not shrunk at every step. The network can learn to hold a value across many steps.

A forget gate near 1 means keep; near 0 means erase. This is the main defence against vanishing gradients. It is not a guarantee. If f_t stays near 0, old information is erased. If σ saturates, its gradient is small. The cell state gives a short gradient path, but training still needs good initialisation and optimisation. See 4.3 for the full gradient computation.

A gated recurrent unit (GRU) uses two gates and no separate cell state. The reset gate r_t controls how much of h_{t-1} enters the candidate. The update gate z_t mixes the old hidden state and the candidate.

z_t = σ(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z)
r_t = σ(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t-1} + b_r)
h~_t = tanh(W_h x_t + U_h (r_t ⊙ h_{t-1}) + b_h)
h_t = (1 − z_t) ⊙ h_{t-1} + z_t ⊙ h~_t
blocks.where: z_t is the update gate; r_t is the reset gate; h~_t is the candidate hidden state; h_t is the new hidden state; W_z, U_z, W_r, U_r, W_h, U_h are weight matrices; b_z, b_r, b_h are bias vectors; σ is the sigmoid; ⊙ is elementwise multiplication. With z_t near 1, h_t is mostly the candidate; with z_t near 0, h_t keeps the old state.

blocks.text: A GRU has fewer parameters than an LSTM, so it can train faster on small data. It has no output gate and no protected cell state, so it may forget differently. Some syllabi call these gated recurrent units. Peephole LSTM lets the gates see c_{t-1} directly; it is an advanced variant, and only a few universities teach it. Neither LSTM nor GRU wins on every task.

figure.caption: Along the cell-state line the forget gate keeps 0.731 × 0.5 = 0.3655 of the old state and the input gate adds 0.622 × 0.762 = 0.474, so c(t) = 0.839. The output gate then lets 0.5 × tanh(0.839) = 0.343 out as h(t).

examples.question: An LSTM cell at time t has forget gate f_t = 0.731, input gate i_t = 0.622, candidate c~_t = 0.762, previous cell state c_{t-1} = 0.5 and output gate o_t = 0.5. Compute c_t and h_t using h_t = o_t·tanh(c_t). Use tanh(0.839) ≈ 0.686.
steps: Write the cell update: c_t = f_t·c_{t-1} + i_t·c~_t.
examples.answer: The new cell state is c_t ≈ 0.839 and the new hidden state is h_t ≈ 0.343.
examples.check:
import math
f = 0.731
i = 0.622
c_tilde = 0.762
c_prev = 0.5
o = 0.5
c_t = f * c_prev + i * c_tilde
h_t = o * math.tanh(c_t)
print('c_t = %.3f' % c_t)
print('h_t = %.3f' % h_t)

traps: Do not add the gates before multiplying: the forget gate multiplies c_{t-1}, and the input gate multiplies c~_t. c_t is the sum of two products.
Do not apply tanh before the output gate multiplies. Use h_t = o_t⊙tanh(c_t), not tanh(o_t⊙c_t).
⊙ is elementwise multiplication. Writing a matrix product changes the gate mechanism and the dimensions.
A forget gate near 1 keeps the old cell state; near 0 erases it. Do not reverse this.
σ and tanh are not interchangeable: gates use σ to give values in (0,1), while the candidate and output squash use tanh to give values in (−1,1).

quiz.q: What does ⊙ denote in the LSTM equations, and what range does σ output?
quiz.a: ⊙ is elementwise multiplication. σ outputs values in the open interval (0,1).

quiz.q: Why does the additive cell-state path with a forget gate near 1 reduce vanishing gradients?
quiz.a: Error can flow from c_t to c_{t-1} through the factor f_t. If f_t is near 1, this factor is near 1, so the error is not repeatedly shrunk by small factors along the cell-state path.

quiz.q: An LSTM has f_t = 0.8, i_t = 0.5, c~_t = −0.6 and c_{t-1} = 0.4. Compute c_t.
Why can a GRU train faster than an LSTM on a small dataset?
quiz.a: A GRU has two gates and no separate cell state, so it has fewer parameters and fewer operations. On small data this can mean faster training and less overfitting, though it may have less ability to protect a cell state over long gaps.

quiz.q: An LSTM has o_t = 0.7 and c_t = 0.5. Use tanh(0.5) = 0.462. Compute h_t.
Name the three gates of an LSTM.
quiz.a: Forget gate, input gate and output gate.

quiz.q: A forget gate stays near 0 for many steps. Does the additive path still guarantee long memory? Explain.
quiz.a: No. If f_t is near 0, the old cell state is multiplied by a small number and is erased. The additive path helps only when the learned forget gate keeps values near 1; it is not a guarantee.

quiz.q: Why does the candidate c~_t use tanh rather than sigmoid?
quiz.a: tanh allows both positive and negative values in (−1,1). Sigmoid gives only positive values in (0,1), which would restrict the candidate to one sign.

beyond: Not for the exam. Peephole LSTM adds direct connections from c_{t-1} to the gates. Layer-normalised LSTMs and GRUs are common in production speech systems. Search for peephole LSTM, GRU variants, layer normalisation in recurrent networks, and gated recurrent units. Newer gated designs such as xLSTM revisit the LSTM idea at larger scale. The gate-and-cell-state pattern also appears in modern sequence models.
